content: Down's syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the presence of three copies of chromosome 21, or a specific region of chromosome 21, instead of the usual two copies. It is the most common congenital cause of intellectual disability. Noninvasive screening methods, such as biochemical analysis of maternal serum or urine and fetal ultrasound measurements, are used to estimate the risk of a pregnancy being affected by Down's syndrome. These screenings help guide decisions about whether to proceed with definitive diagnostic testing. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the accuracy of second-trimester serum markers in detecting Down's syndrome. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, CINAHL, and others, covering studies published up to May 2007. The search also included reference lists and review articles. The studies selected for analysis involved maternal serum tests performed between 14 and 24 weeks of gestation, with results compared to a reference standard such as chromosomal verification or postnatal inspection. Data from the studies were extracted to calculate detection rates (sensitivity) and false positive rates (1-specificity). The quality of the studies was assessed using the QUADAS criteria. Hierarchical summary ROC meta-analytical methods were used to analyze test performance and compare the accuracy of different tests. Subgroup analyses were conducted to examine the impact of maternal age on test performance. A total of 59 studies involving 341,261 pregnancies, including 1,994 cases of Down's syndrome, were included in the analysis. The studies were generally of high quality, although there was a tendency for invasive testing to be performed only in high-risk pregnancies, leading to differential verification. Seventeen studies directly compared different tests. In total, 54 test combinations were evaluated, involving 12 different markers and maternal age. These markers included alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), unconjugated estriol (uE3), total human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), free beta human chorionic gonadotropin (βhCG), free alpha human chorionic gonadotropin (αhCG), inhibin A, SP2, CA125, troponin, pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A), placental growth factor (PGF), and proform of eosinophil major basic protein (ProMBP). The meta-analysis of the 12 best-performing or most frequently evaluated test combinations showed that double and triple marker tests (involving AFP, uE3, total hCG, and free βhCG) were significantly more effective than individual markers. These tests detected six to seven out of every 10 Down's syndrome pregnancies at a 5% false positive rate. Tests that included inhibin A performed the best, detecting eight out of every 10 Down's syndrome pregnancies, but they were not shown to be significantly better than standard triple marker tests in direct comparisons. The sensitivity of the tests was significantly lower in women over the age of 35. In this age group, women who miscarried were more likely to have undergone invasive testing to confirm a negative screening result, whereas women under 35 were less likely to receive invasive testing for a negative result. This discrepancy in testing practices led to underestimation of screening results in younger women, potentially missing some affected pregnancies and impacting the accuracy of sensitivity estimates. The authors concluded that tests involving two or more markers combined with maternal age are significantly more sensitive than tests using a single marker. However, the benefit of combining four or more markers or including inhibin A has not been proven to provide a statistically significant improvement. Further research is needed to investigate the reduced test performance in women over 35 and the effect of differential pregnancy loss on study findings.
